      Accessibility an afterthought at this year’s Winterlude, advocates say

      People with disabilities say this year’s Winterlude wasn’t designed with accessibility in mind, barring people with mobility challenges from one of the festival's main attractions.

      Boardwalk installed in park Monday after 2nd of festival's 3 weekends

      Jodie Applewaithe · CBC News · Posted: Feb 10, 2026 10:12 AM EST | Last Updated: 8 hours ago
      Listen to this article
      Estimated 4 minutes
      The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

      ‘It made me feel excluded’: Woman with accessibility needs says she couldn’t visit Winterlude ice sculptures

      1 hour ago|
      Duration 2:58
      Linda Paul told CBC’s Jodie Applewaithe she was twice unable to get past the entrance to the exhibit at Confederation Park with her mobility scooter.

      Social Sharing

      People with disabilities say this year’s Winterlude wasn’t designed with accessibility in mind, barring people with mobility challenges from one of the festival's main attractions.

      Linda Paul has been attending the Ottawa-Gatineau winter festival for 28 years, but said she left feeling frustrated after visiting Confederation Park during its first two weekends this year.

      Paul wanted to explore the Crystal Garden, an outdoor exhibition featuring ice sculptures, but said she couldn’t see the artwork because both times she showed up there was no accessible pathway she could get across with her mobility scooter.

      She tried maneuvering her device through the snow, then ended up getting stuck and had to have another visitor help dig her out.

      “It made me feel excluded,” Paul said of her experience. “It isolates you and you can’t go to events with your friends.”

      Cathy Malcolm Edwards, the lead of Carleton University’s co-ordinated accessibility strategy, uses a rollator walking aid. She was planning to go to Winterlude but heard about the issues Paul described and instead avoided the attraction.

      “Not having a path is sending a message to people like myself that this isn’t a space that you’re necessarily welcome to," she said.

      As CBC News was leaving Confederation Park on Monday afternoon, crews were installing metal-like panels and rubber mats at the Crystal Garden’s entrance. 

      In a statement, festival organizers in the Department of Canadian Heritage described it as a “temporary boardwalk” and said the structure had already been installed underneath the tents where the ice sculptures are located.

      “We’ve now extended it for it to reach the existing, permanent pathway,” the department wrote.

      The move came 10 days after the start of Winterlude on Jan. 30. CBC asked Canadian Heritage if the decision to extend the boardwalk was a response to the broadcaster’s inquiries, but the department did not respond by deadline.

      ‘It shouldn’t be an afterthought’ 

      Paul and Malcolm Edwards said they were pleased to see the temporary path installed, but they both wish the festival organizers consulted people with disabilities and had an accessibility plan while preparing for the event.

      “Accessibility should be integral to every event and festival,” said Paul. “It shouldn’t be an afterthought.”

      “For many years, they had accessible pathways and when it was on Sparks Street [the sculptures were] completely accessible,” she recalled. “Now they’ve taken a step backwards.”

      • Winterlude ice carving returning to Confederation Park

      Paul shared an email with CBC that she sent to Canadian Heritage on Jan. 30, the first day of Winterlude, asking if the same “painted plywoods [pathways]” that she remembered would be put in place.

      A spokesperson with the department responded to Paul’s inquiry on Feb. 3, suggesting "the ramps" would be installed for the second weekend of the festival.

      While Paul looks forward to testing the temporary boardwalk, the director of programs for the Ottawa charity Able2 said that kind of solution shouldn’t become the norm at future festivals.

      “They should ensure … that accessibility is treated as an essential infrastructure, not as an optional addition that can be eliminated,” said Thony Jean-Baptiste.

      In its statement to CBC News, Canadian Heritage said the department strives to make Winterlude as inclusive and accessible as possible, and that the department encourages visitors who have difficulty accessing certain areas to note their concerns with its on-site staff.

      Winterlude runs until Monday, Feb. 16.
